newsitem.title: CUBA: Panama firm to stay in Cuba despite U.S. warning.
newsitem.headline: Panama firm to stay in Cuba despite U.S. warning.

text.p: A Panamanian firm that distributes Mitsubishi, Lada and other vehicles in Cuba has said it plans to stay on despite a warning from U.S. authorities that it could be violating the tightened U.S. economic embargo against Havana.

Martin Rodin, president of Motores Internacionales del Caribe S.A. (MICSA), said the firm received a warning letter on Jan. 14 from the State Department saying the company could be in violation of the Helms-Burton Act passed last year.

Speaking at a news conference on Friday, Rodin said the problem should now be resolved since the company has moved out of a property that had caused the problem. MICSA was awaiting confirmation of this from the State Department, he said.
Rodin stressed that the decision to move offices had not been prompted by the letter, but was a business decision.
Helms-Burton seeks to discourage foreign investment in Cuba with provisions that punish firms deemed to be profiting from property seized after the 1959 revolution led by Fidel Castro.

One provision, applied last year to Canadian mining firm Sherritt International Corp and to Mexican telecommunications company Grupo Domos, bars executives of firms found to be doing business on such property from entering the United States.
At issue in the case of the Panamanian firm, formerly operating in Cuba as Motores Internacionales S.A. (MOINSA), was its Havana office, a property rented from the Cuban government.
A Cuban-American reportedly complained to U.S. authorities that the property belonged to his father before it was expropriated, prompting the U.S. warning.
Rodin said the firm moved its office to a larger property in recent weeks. But he said this was not in response to the letter but because the firm was expanding and needed more space.
Rodin stressed that his firm viewed the U.S. warning as unacceptable since MICSA, being a Panamanian firm, was bound by the laws of Panama and Cuba, and not those of the United States.
Rodin said MICSA was a new firm created from the sale three weeks ago of MOINSA to Russian firm Autovaz. He did not suggest the sale was related to the warning from the State Department.

MICSA now distributes Mitsubishi, Subaru and Lada vehicles, as well as Bridgestone tires and some vehicles spares in Cuba. MOINSA, now owned by Autovaz, distributes Lada and Kamaz vehicles in Latin America except Cuba, he said.
